subject: Career
title: The Curse of Knowledge
description: One-minute skill: The Curse of Knowledge.

hook.text: You explain the project perfectly. Your colleague nods. Then does it completely wrong. What happened?

buildup.text: The curse of knowledge: once you know something, you can't imagine not knowing it.

discovery.text: Chip and Dan Heath describe this in 'Made to Stick' — experts communicate in jargon and abstractions.

twist.text: The 'tapping study' proved it: tappers hear a song in their head; listeners hear random tapping. Same gap.

climax.text: The fix: communicate at the audience's level. Ask: 'What does someone who doesn't know this need to hear?'

punchline.text: Knowing more can make you worse at explaining. Fight the curse.

quiz.question: What is the curse of knowledge?
options: Inability to imagine not knowing something you know
Knowing too much about a topic

details.summary: The curse of knowledge is a cognitive bias where experts unconsciously assume their audience shares their background knowledge. This leads to jargon-heavy explanations, skipped foundational steps, and frustrated colleagues who feel lost but hesitate to ask for clarification.
details.whyItMatters: Miscommunication caused by assumed knowledge wastes time and creates errors. Recognizing this bias helps leaders craft messages that reach all audience levels effectively.
takeaways: Experts routinely overestimate what their audience already knows
Using analogies and plain language bridges the knowledge gap
Testing your message with a non-expert catches blind spots early

faq.question: How can I tell if I am suffering from the curse of knowledge?
faq.answer: If colleagues frequently ask you to clarify, if your emails generate many follow-up questions, or if meeting attendees seem confused after your presentations, you are likely over-assuming shared context. Ask a junior team member to review your next draft.

faq.question: What techniques help overcome this bias when explaining technical topics?
faq.answer: Start with the big picture before diving into details. Use concrete analogies tied to everyday experience. Define acronyms on first use. And explicitly invite questions by saying something like 'I may be skipping steps, so please ask.'
